en.name: Barnabas
en.summary: Cypriot Jewish Christian who introduced the newly converted Paul to the apostles in Jerusalem and became his early missionary companion.
en.body: Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus, originally named Joseph, whom the apostles nicknamed Barnabas, meaning "son of encouragement," after he sold property he owned and gave the proceeds to support the earliest Jerusalem Christian community. When the recently converted Paul, still viewed with deep suspicion by the Jerusalem church because of his history persecuting Christians, arrived in the city, it was Barnabas who vouched for him and brought him to meet the apostles, a crucial act of trust that opened the door to Paul's acceptance into the Christian community. The two went on to undertake missionary journeys together, including a significant mission to Antioch and Cyprus recorded in Acts, before a sharp disagreement over whether to bring the younger missionary John Mark on a subsequent journey led the two friends to part ways and continue their missionary work separately. Tradition holds he continued preaching in Cyprus, where he is honored as founder of the Cypriot Church, and was eventually martyred there.
